target_learner: 12th-grade graduate, India, limited English vocabulary, non-English-medium background, zero prior AI/ML knowledge

checks.statement: Every factual claim about how RAG works (retrieval, embeddings, vector search, generation) is technically correct. No invented statistics, no invented tool/product names, no claim that cannot be traced to established RAG concepts.
fail_examples: Says RAG 'trains a new model on your documents' (it does not, by default)
Invents a fake benchmark number like '94% more accurate'
checks.pass_rule: PASS only if the evaluator LLM finds zero factual errors and zero unverifiable invented claims. Any single error = FAIL.

checks.statement: Sentences are short (mostly under ~20 words), use common everyday words, and avoid compound/nested clauses that require re-reading.
fail_examples: Long academic sentences with multiple subordinate clauses
checks.pass_rule: PASS only if the evaluator finds no sentence that a learner with limited English vocabulary would need to re-read twice. Any such sentence = FAIL.

checks.statement: The lesson includes at least one concrete, walked-through example (a real-feeling scenario, e.g. a chatbot answering from a company handbook) that shows the concept in action, not just an abstract definition.
fail_examples: Only defines RAG in the abstract with no scenario
Mentions an example exists but doesn't actually walk through it step by step
checks.pass_rule: PASS only if at least one fully worked example is present and traceable step-by-step. Zero examples, or an example that isn't actually walked through = FAIL.

checks.statement: Every technical term used (e.g. embedding, vector database, token, LLM, retrieval, hallucination) is defined in plain language at first use, before or immediately after it appears.
fail_examples: Uses 'embedding' without ever explaining what it means
Defines a term once but then uses 3 more undefined terms later
checks.pass_rule: PASS only if every technical term has a plain-language explanation at first use. Even one undefined term = FAIL.

checks.statement: The lesson explicitly covers all three required pillars: (1) WHAT RAG is, (2) WHY it matters / what problem it solves, (3) HOW it works (the retrieve-then-generate mechanism, at least at a high level).
fail_examples: Explains what RAG is but never explains why it's needed
Explains why it's useful but skips the how
checks.pass_rule: PASS only if all three pillars are explicitly, identifiably present. Missing any one pillar = FAIL.

checks.statement: Ideas build in a logical teaching order (motivation -> concept -> mechanism -> example -> recap), each section can be understood using only what came before it, and there is a short recap/summary at the end.
fail_examples: Introduces the example before explaining the concept it illustrates
Jumps between topics and back again
checks.pass_rule: PASS only if a first-time reader could follow section-to-section without needing to jump ahead or re-read earlier sections, and a recap exists. Any violation = FAIL.

ship_rule: The lesson SHIPS only when ALL checks above return PASS. Any single FAIL blocks shipping and triggers regeneration with the specific failure reasons fed back to the generator.
